fixes.explanation: The fortieth year it is, friend. Moses speaks "In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month…" (Deuteronomy 1:3). The text even gives the day. Then it says Moses proclaimed to the Israelites all that the LORD had commanded him concerning them.

Second year is a fair guess, but the text says fortieth. Moses speaks "In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month…" (Deuteronomy 1:3). Forty is a big number. Even my longest wait in a drawer never came with a date that exact.

Explain is the word, baker. In the land of Moab, "…Moses began to explain this law…" (Deuteronomy 1:5). He begins to explain it, and then he starts speaking. Think of a good teacher with a whiteboard.

Change is a sneaky one, but the text says Moses "…began to explain this law…" (Deuteronomy 1:5). Explain is the word it uses. If I swapped ingredients every time I explained a recipe, nobody would trust my cookies.
Shorten sounds tidy, baker, but the text says Moses "…began to explain this law…" (Deuteronomy 1:5). Shortening and explaining are two different jobs. When I shorten a cookie, all I get is crumbs.

That's the one. Moses recalls what the LORD told them at Horeb: "You have stayed at this mountain long enough." (Deuteronomy 1:6). Next comes the word to resume their journey. I know that feeling, friend. Some of us need a voice at the door to tell us it's time to leave the drawer.

Noah, Noah's son Shem and Noah's son Japheth are real names from Genesis (Genesis 5:32), but they aren't the ones here. The LORD swore the land to "…your fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob…" (Deuteronomy 1:8). Those are the fathers named in this promise. Good names, though, just not the ones in this verse.

Two camps is a fair guess, but the text never mentions splitting anybody. It says the LORD "…has multiplied you, so that today you are as numerous as the stars in the sky." (Deuteronomy 1:10). The verse is about how many they are. Stars in the sky, friend. That's a LOT of people.

No lots and no single new leader here. Moses says, "Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes…" (Deuteronomy 1:13). That's men, plural, from each tribe. Nothing in the text about drawing lots.

It's actually true, friend. Moses tells the people, "Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes, and I will appoint them as your leaders." (Deuteronomy 1:13). That "I" is Moses, and he's promising the appointing part. Half the job is theirs and half is his. Moses just finished saying he couldn't do all of it alone.

That's how he sets it up. Moses appoints them "…as commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, and as officers for your tribes." (Deuteronomy 1:15). Big groups, smaller groups, tiny groups, all the way down to tens. That's a lot of rungs on one ladder, friend.

Twelve equal leaders sounds tidy, but that's not it. The text says Moses appoints them "…as commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, and as officers for your tribes." (Deuteronomy 1:15). Those ranks step down from thousands to tens. Equal rank would mean no steps at all, and this verse has four.

God is the answer. Moses tells the judges, "Do not be intimidated by anyone, for judgment belongs to God." (Deuteronomy 1:17). He gives them that reason right alongside the command. He also tells them to show no partiality and to hear small and great alike.

Elders is a reasonable guess, since leaders are all over this passage. But the text says, "…for judgment belongs to God." (Deuteronomy 1:17). That's the reason Moses gives for not being intimidated by anyone. Nice try, baker.

It's actually true, friend. Moses says, "And bring to me any case too difficult for you, and I will hear it." (Deuteronomy 1:17). The text has Moses saying he will hear the cases that are too difficult for the judges. So the judges know where the hard ones go.
